questions.question: A researcher wants to study the average sleep time of all Grade 9 students in British Columbia. She collects data from 300 students at 12 schools. In this study, what is the population?
options: The 300 students who answered the survey
The 12 schools where data was collected
All Grade 9 students in British Columbia
All students in British Columbia of any grade
questions.explain: The population is the ENTIRE group you want to learn about (all Grade 9 students in BC), while the 300 students are the sample. The common trap is picking the number you see in the problem, but that number is the sample, not the population.

questions.question: A café owner wants to know what her customers think about a new price. She stands at the register and asks only the people in line. What is the main sampling problem?
options: She only surveys people already at the café, so she misses customers who stopped coming because of the price
The sample is too large for a small café
The café is in a small town
The customers might be too tired to answer honestly
questions.explain: A convenience sample (people right in front of you) is biased because it excludes the very people who may have a different opinion, like those who left over the price. The trap is thinking the issue is sample size, when it is really WHO is included.

questions.question: A politician says, 'In our survey of 20 people, 18 support my plan, so almost everyone agrees.' What is the biggest problem with using this result?
options: The 20 people were not listed in alphabetical order
A sample of 20 is far too small to represent a whole community, and the selection method is unknown
18 out of 20 is not a valid fraction
The survey was conducted on a weekday instead of a weekend
questions.explain: A sample of 20 cannot reliably represent thousands of people, and we do not even know how those 20 were chosen. The trap is getting distracted by the 90% figure and missing that the sample is far too small and the method is unknown.

questions.question: A class wants to collect data on how much money each student spends on lunch each week. Before collecting the data, what is the MOST important ethical step?
options: Design a colourful bar chart to display the results
Choose the most creative method to collect the data
Collect the data on a Wednesday so it is mid-week
Explain what data will be collected, get each student's consent, and keep the information private
questions.explain: Ethics in data collection means being transparent, getting consent (permission), and protecting privacy. The trap is focusing on presentation or timing, which are not ethical concerns at all.

questions.question: A hospital in Kelowna wants to estimate the average wait time in its emergency room. Which sampling method would be LEAST biased?
options: Recording the wait time for every patient who arrives on 5 randomly chosen weekdays
Surveying only the patients who are the angriest at the front desk
Asking the nurses what they think the average wait is
Surveying only patients who arrive before 9 a.m.
questions.explain: Randomly selecting days and recording EVERY patient on those days gives a fair cross-section. The other options all introduce bias: angry patients, staff opinions, or only early arrivals. The trap is trusting the nurses because they are 'experts,' but their perception is not the actual data.

questions.question: A Statistics Canada chart shows the median household income in a small BC town rose from $62,000 in 2019 to $64,500 in 2024. A blog post titles this 'Incomes SOAR 40% in five years!' What is wrong with the blog's claim?
options: The years 2019 and 2024 are not five years apart
Median income cannot be measured in dollars
The actual increase is about 4%, not 40%; the word 'SOAR' and the 40% figure are misleading
The blog should have used the mean instead of the median
questions.explain: The real increase is ($64,500 − $62,000) ÷ $62,000 ≈ 4.0%, not 40%. The blog likely confused 4 with 40. The trap is accepting a dramatic percentage without doing the division yourself; always verify the calculation.

questions.question: A government agency tests water quality at 5 locations along the coast of Haida Gwaii to assess whether First Nations communities can safely drink the water. The 5 test sites were chosen by the agency, not by the communities. What is a potential problem with this approach?
options: Testing 5 sites is too few to be useful at all
The agency may have chosen sites that look good, missing contaminated areas the community knows about
Testing water is too expensive for only 5 sites
First Nations communities do not drink from local water sources
questions.explain: When the decision-makers choose the sampling locations, they may avoid areas where problems are already known. Involving the community in site selection (or using a random or stratified method) reduces this bias. The trap is thinking the number of sites is the issue, when it is really WHO chose WHERE.

questions.question: A small town in BC wants to survey all 12,000 residents about a new bike-lane plan. They mail a paper survey to every household and 1,400 people return it. The returned surveys show 80% support. What is the most likely reason the true support level might differ?
options: 1,400 is not a round number
The paper surveys were printed in the wrong language
Bike lanes do not affect all residents equally
People who strongly oppose the plan are more likely to ignore the survey, so the sample is skewed toward supporters
questions.explain: This is non-response bias: with only about 12% response, the people who bother to reply tend to have strong feelings, and those feelings may not match the silent majority. The trap is fixating on the raw number 1,400 instead of asking WHO chose to respond and why.

questions.question: A social-media company in Vancouver posts: 'We surveyed 500 of our users (ages 13–17) and found that 92% want a new privacy feature. Therefore, ALL teenagers in Canada want this feature.' Identify the TWO main problems with this conclusion.
options: The sample only included users of that one company's app (a limited, self-selected group), and a sample result suggests a trend but cannot PROVE what ALL teens want
92% is too high a number to be accurate, and ages 13–17 is the wrong age range for a survey
The survey was done in Vancouver instead of Toronto, and 500 is too small a sample
The privacy feature was not free, and the survey was done on a Monday
questions.explain: Two separate errors: (1) the sampling frame is restricted to users of ONE app, so it cannot represent all Canadian teens, and (2) the word 'ALL' turns an estimate into an absolute claim. The trap is nitpicking the sample size (500 is reasonable) instead of noticing the narrow, non-random sampling frame.

questions.question: A local news report says: 'Crime in Nanaimo jumped 12.5% — from 1,200 to 1,350 incidents — making it one of the fastest-growing cities in BC for crime!' The city's population grew from 68,000 to 71,000 in the same period. What is the strongest criticism of the news headline?
options: The 12.5% figure is wrong because 150 ÷ 1200 does not equal 12.5%
The 12.5% rise in total incidents partly reflects about 4% population growth, so the per-resident rate rose only about 8%, and the claim 'fastest-growing' is not supported by the data alone
Crime in BC cannot be measured in number of incidents; it must be measured in dollars
The population of Nanaimo cannot legally exceed 70,000
questions.explain: The 12.5% raw increase is arithmetically correct, but part of it is simply more people. Adjusting for population (1,200/68,000 → 1,350/71,000) gives a per-capita rise of roughly 8%, and 'fastest-growing' requires comparing every BC city, which was not done. The trap is rejecting the 12.5% number as 'wrong' when the real issue is missing context.

questions.question: A research team from a mainland university wants to study water quality in a remote First Nations community in northern BC. They plan to collect water samples, publish the data in a journal, and use the results to argue for more government funding. The community elder says, 'You can test the water, but the results belong to our people first.' Which option BEST reflects the ethical concern raised?
options: The university should test the water at night so the community is asleep
The water samples should be tested twice to confirm accuracy
The community has the right to see, approve, and control how the data is used before it is published or shared publicly
The university must pay the community a fee for each litre of water collected
questions.explain: Indigenous data sovereignty means the community owns the data collected about or on their land, and publishing or using it without prior consent and approval is an ethical violation. The trap is focusing on technical steps (timing, testing twice) when the real issue is WHO controls the data and how it is shared.

questions.question: A pharmaceutical company in Burnaby publishes: 'In our trial of 200 patients, 95% reported feeling better after taking our new vitamin supplement. This proves the supplement cures chronic pain.' Which option identifies ALL the main problems with this claim?
options: 95% is too high a percentage to be believable, and 200 patients is too many for a clinical trial
The patients should have been 400, not 200, and the vitamin should be taken with food
The study was done in Burnaby, so it cannot apply to other cities in BC

The word 'proves' overstates a sample result, self-reported 'feeling better' in a company-run trial is vulnerable to placebo effect, and the participants are only from one company's group, not a random population sample
questions.explain: Three distinct issues: (1) a sample suggests but does not PROVE; (2) in a company-run trial, self-report is vulnerable to placebo effect and social-desirability bias; (3) the sampling frame is restricted to people who chose that one trial. The trap is arguing about the number 200 or the city, missing the language ('proves'), the self-report bias, and the limited sampling frame.
